19th century. The integration of distributed energy resources (DERs), proliferation of smart 
metering infrastructure (AMI), rapid growth of intermittent renewable generation, and emergence of 
transactive energy markets are collectively redefining how electricity is generated, transmitted, 
distributed, and consumed. Smart grid technologies and demand response programs sit at the 
nexus of this transformation, enabling bidirectional communication, dynamic pricing, and flexible 
load management at unprecedented scale.

full smart grid deployment could reduce electricity consumption by 12% and peak demand by up to

demand-side resources in North America as of 2024, a figure expected to grow to 80 GW by 2030.

program structures, grid-interactive building technologies, virtual power plant (VPP) platforms, and 
the emerging transactive energy paradigm. It provides performance benchmarks, implementation 
guidance, case studies, and a forward-looking assessment of AI-driven grid optimization and the 
role of distributed flexibility in supporting 80% renewable electricity targets.

power system characterized by: (1) 15% of U.S. electricity from variable wind and solar (on track for 
30% by 2030); (2) 3.5 million distributed solar installations injecting power back into distribution 
circuits; (3) 6 million electric vehicles creating new, large, and unpredictable load centers; and (4) 
consumer expectations"}]
